description: Learn Python from zero in 4 weeks. You start by running your first program and finish by building a small project of your own. Each week has short lessons with code you can type and run, and you practise as you go. Free to learn. Finish a short quiz and a small project to earn your Techive certificate, then continue to Django to build full web apps.
project_brief:
Build a small Python program that solves a real problem. Choose one idea:

1. Shop calculator: ask for item names and prices, store them in a list or dictionary, show the total and apply a discount if the total is above a limit you choose.
2. Student marks manager: store names and marks, show the average, the highest mark and each student's grade.
3. Number guessing game with a limited number of tries.

Requirements: use input(), at least one function, a loop, an if/else and a list or dictionary; handle wrong input without crashing (try/except); add comments explaining the main parts.

Submit: a link to your code (GitHub, Google Colab or a shared Google Doc) and in the notes a sentence on how to run it.

lessons.title: What is programming and why Python?
lessons.body:
A program is a list of instructions a computer follows. Python is a popular language because it reads almost like English, so beginners can start quickly. It is used for websites (with Django), data analysis, automation, AI and more.

A programmer's real skill is breaking a problem into small clear steps. Writing the code is the second half of the job.

Example of a Python program:

print("Hello, Kenya!")

This one line tells the computer to show the text Hello, Kenya! on the screen.

Try it: write down, in plain steps, how you would make a cup of tea. That is what an algorithm looks like.

lessons.title: Set up Python and run code
lessons.body:
You can run Python in two ways:

1. Online (easiest): use a free online Python editor such as Google Colab or Replit. Nothing to install; you need only a browser.
2. On your computer: download Python from python.org, install it (tick "Add Python to PATH" on Windows), then write code in a file ending in .py and run it with: python myfile.py

In an online editor, type the line below and press Run:

print("My first program")

If you see an error message, read it slowly. It usually tells you the line number and what is wrong.

Try it: run your first program, then change the text and run it again.

lessons.title: Variables, data types, print and input
lessons.body:
A variable is a name that stores a value.

name = "Amina"
age = 17
height = 1.62
is_student = True

Common types: str (text), int (whole numbers), float (decimals) and bool (True or False). The function type() tells you which one a value is.

Show values with print(). Get input from the user with input(), which always returns text:

name = input("Your name: ")
age = int(input("Your age: "))
print("Hello", name, "you are", age)

Use int() or float() to convert text into numbers.

Try it: ask for two numbers and print their sum.

lessons.title: Operators and if / else decisions
lessons.body:
Arithmetic operators: + - * / (divide), // (whole-number divide), % (remainder), ** (power).
Comparison operators: == (equal), != (not equal), > < >= <=.
Logic: and, or, not.

Decisions use if, elif and else. Indentation (4 spaces) is part of Python's syntax:

mark = 72
if mark >= 80:
    print("A")
elif mark >= 60:
    print("B")
else:
    print("Keep trying")

Notice == compares, while = stores a value.

Try it: ask for a mark and print the grade using your own grade boundaries.

lessons.title: Loops: repeating things
lessons.body:
A for loop repeats a set number of times or goes through items:

for i in range(3):
    print(i)

range(3) gives 0, 1, 2. A while loop repeats as long as a condition is True:

count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count = count - 1

Take care: if the condition never becomes False, the loop never stops. Use break to leave a loop early and continue to skip to the next round.

Try it: print the multiplication table of any number from 1 to 12.

lessons.title: Lists: storing many values
lessons.body:
A list holds several values in order.

prices = [120, 80, 200]
print(prices[0])   # first item, 120
prices.append(50)  # add to the end
print(len(prices)) # how many items

Items are counted from 0. Useful tools: sum(prices), max(prices), min(prices), sorted(prices) and the in test (80 in prices).

Loop through a list:

total = 0
for p in prices:
    total = total + p
print(total)

Try it: make a list of 5 marks and print the total and the average.

lessons.title: Functions: reusable blocks of code
lessons.body:
A function packages steps under a name so you can reuse them.

def add_vat(price):
    return price * 1.16

print(add_vat(1000))

def defines the function, price is a parameter, and return sends a result back. Give functions clear names and keep each one to a single job. Variables created inside a function stay inside it.

You can give a parameter a default value:

def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return greeting + ", " + name

Try it: write a function that takes a mark and returns a grade, then call it for three marks.

lessons.title: Dictionaries and tuples
lessons.body:
A dictionary stores pairs of key and value.

student = {"name": "Brian", "mark": 68}
print(student["name"])
student["mark"] = 75
student["age"] = 19

Loop through it:

for key, value in student.items():
    print(key, value)

A tuple is like a list that cannot be changed: point = (3, 4). Use a dictionary when you want to look things up by name, for example prices = {"bread": 60, "milk": 55}.

Try it: make a price dictionary for 4 items and print the price of one chosen by the user.

lessons.title: Working with text and files
lessons.body:
Strings have useful methods:

text = "  Techive Academy "
print(text.strip())     # removes spaces at the ends
print(text.upper())
print(text.replace("Academy", "School"))
print("Tech" in text)    # True

f-strings build text neatly:

name = "Amina"
print(f"Welcome, {name}!")

Save and read a text file:

with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Hello file")

with open("notes.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())

The with statement closes the file for you. Mode "w" writes (and replaces), "a" adds to the end, and "r" reads.

Try it: ask for a name and save it to a file, then read it back.

modules.title: Week 4: Errors, modules and your project

lessons.title: Handling errors with try / except
lessons.body:
Errors happen, especially when users type unexpected things. Without protection the program stops:

age = int(input("Age: "))   # typing 'abc' crashes this

Use try and except:

try:
    age = int(input("Age: "))
    print("Next year you will be", age + 1)
except ValueError:
    print("Please type a number.")

Common errors: SyntaxError (typo in the code), NameError (name not defined), TypeError (wrong kind of value), ZeroDivisionError and IndexError (position does not exist).

Read the last line of an error message first. It tells you the type and the reason.

Try it: make a loop that keeps asking for a number until the user types a valid one.

lessons.title: Modules and a small program
lessons.body:
A module is code written by someone else that you can import.

import random
secret = random.randint(1, 10)
print(secret)

Other useful modules: math (math.sqrt(16)), datetime (dates and times) and json. Thousands more can be installed with pip, for example: pip install requests.

Here is a tiny guessing game that uses what you learned:

import random
secret = random.randint(1, 10)
for tries in range(3):
    guess = int(input("Guess 1-10: "))
    if guess == secret:
        print("Correct!")
        break
else:
    print("The number was", secret)

Try it: type it in, run it, then change the range and the number of tries.

lessons.title: Your final project and the road to Django
lessons.body:
Time to build. Choose one of the project ideas in the project brief on this page: a shop calculator, a student marks manager or a guessing game. Plan first in plain steps, write a little, run it, and fix errors as you go. Add comments (lines starting with #) that explain the main parts.

Good habits: use clear variable names, keep functions small and test with different inputs, including wrong ones.

When the tutor approves your project and you pass the quiz, you can get your certificate.

What next? Django is a Python framework for building complete web applications such as login systems, databases and dashboards. It is the next step in the Techive Academy path, and it builds directly on the Python you learned here.

quiz.text: Which is a valid variable assignment?
What type of value does input() always return?
What is the output of: print(7 // 2)?
What is the output of: print(7 % 3)?
Which symbol COMPARES two values for equality?
How many times does this print? for i in range(4): print(i)

What is the output? def add(a, b):
    return a + b
print(add(2, 3))
Given student = {"name": "Amina", "mark": 70}, what does student["mark"] give?
Which line opens a file for reading safely and closes it automatically?
Which statement catches a ValueError such as int("abc")?
Which line imports the random module?
